pageTitle: AWS CloudHSM Command Line Interface (CLI) supported platforms
whatThePageStates: The page lists the operating-system platforms on which the AWS CloudHSM CLI runs. It has exactly two content sections. "Linux support" is a three-column table of 8 Linux distributions/versions, with a Yes/No cell for X86_64 architecture and for ARM architecture; every one of the 16 cells reads Yes. Four trailing bullets are release-history notes naming platforms whose support ENDED at a given SDK release (Ubuntu 20.04 LTS, CentOS 7, Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7, CentOS 8). "Windows support" is a plain bullet list of 4 Microsoft Windows Server versions with no architecture column and no Yes/No column at all. The page makes no statement about Regions, AWS services, or resource types.

features.featureName: Linux support (AWS CloudHSM CLI supported platforms)
features.statuses: 8 table rows, each with two architecture cells. X86_64: 8 Yes, 0 No. ARM: 8 Yes, 0 No. Total cells 8x2 = 16, all Yes; 16 Yes + 0 No = 16. Every value is the literal word "Yes" in the table body; the table contains no "No", no blank, and no Partial cell, so not-supported is NEVER STATED inside this table. The four bullets under the table (Ubuntu 20.04 LTS, CentOS 7 (7.8+), Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7 (7.8+), CentOS 8) are end-of-support history phrased as "SDK X was the last release to provide ... support" — they are a stated withdrawal of support for 4 further platforms, not rows of the matrix, and they carry no architecture breakdown. If a measurement wants a not-supported count from this page it can only come from those 4 bullets, and it must be labelled as end-of-life history, not as a No cell.
features.scope: cpuArchitecture, with exactly 2 values: X86_64 Architecture and ARM architecture. The claim unit is (operating system x architecture); both architecture columns happen to be identical here (all Yes), but the page does assert them separately.
features.reasoning: The thing enumerated down the rows is an operating system distribution/version — an external universe that exists independently of CloudHSM — and the coverage claim is "the CloudHSM CLI runs on this OS". The two columns are not two different capabilities; they are the same capability qualified by processor architecture, so architecture is the scope, not the axis. 8 is the row count and also the count of distinct OS versions named, so rows do not collapse.

features.featureName: Windows support (AWS CloudHSM CLI supported platforms)
features.statuses: 4 bullets: Microsoft Windows Server 2016, 2019, 2022, 2025. All 4 are supported by virtue of appearing under the heading "Windows support"; 4 Yes + 0 No = 4. There is no table, no Yes/No column, no architecture column and no Partial value in this section. Not-supported is entirely ABSENT here — no Windows version is stated as unsupported, and older or client Windows editions are simply not mentioned, which is not a coverage claim.
features.scope: None. Unlike the Linux table, this section gives no architecture breakdown and no other second dimension.
features.reasoning: Same axis and same capability as the Linux section (which OS the CLI runs on), but the page states it in a structurally different way, so the count and the status semantics differ: a bullet list of supported items yields presence-only Yes, while the Linux table yields explicit per-architecture Yes cells. Keeping them as two features preserves that difference; merging them into a single count of 12 would silently give the 4 Windows entries an architecture claim the page never makes.

shouldNotExtract: Not coverage: the H1 and the two H2 headings; the table's own header row ("Supported platforms | X86_64 Architecture | ARM architecture") — that is a legend, not a platform; the four end-of-life bullets under the Linux table (Ubuntu 20.04 LTS, CentOS 7, RHEL 7, CentOS 8) must not be counted as SUPPORTED platforms, since they state the opposite; the SDK version numbers in those bullets (5.16, 5.12, 5.4.2) are release identifiers, not axis values or counts; the external vendor links (ubuntu.com, centos.org, redhat.com); the <a name="..."> anchor artifacts such as w2aac23c15c11b5; and the entire "See also" block about AI-coding-assistant skills and the aws agent-toolkit search-skills command, which is boilerplate and says nothing about platform coverage.
coverageDimensions: REGION: nothing. The page never names a Region, a Region code, or a partition, and gives no per-Region availability. Any regional figure attributed to this page is fabricated. SERVICE: nothing enumerable. The page is about one service (AWS CloudHSM) and its CLI; it does not enumerate AWS services, so a service-coverage count of 1 or of anything else is not supported by the page. RESOURCE TYPE: nothing. No AWS resource types appear anywhere on the page. What the page DOES give is operating-system coverage: 8 Linux versions across 2 CPU architectures, and 4 Windows Server versions.
trap: The single most likely misparse is counting cells instead of platforms — reading the Linux table as 16 (or 24 including the platform-name column) supported items rather than 8 operating systems assessed on 2 architectures. Runners-up: (1) harvesting the four end-of-support bullets as supported platforms because they sit directly under the table and name real distributions, which would inflate Linux from 8 to 12 and invert the meaning for those 4; (2) merging Linux and Windows into one 12-row operatingSystem axis and implying the Windows entries carry X86_64/ARM Yes values the page never states; (3) reporting a not-supported count of 0 as if the page explicitly denied support for anything — the table has no No cells at all, so any "No" here comes only from the end-of-life notes; (4) treating X86_64 and ARM as two separate features/capabilities rather than a scope; (5) mistaking the "See also" agent-toolkit paragraph for a supported-integration claim.
